newsitem.title: MEXICO: Israeli freed after 39-day kidnap ordeal in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Israeli freed after 39-day kidnap ordeal in Mexico.

text.p: An Israeli agricultural specialist was freed from a 39-day kidnap ordeal in western Mexico, authorities said late on Wednesday, and a self-proclaimed "troubleshooter" from New York said he got him out.

Uri-Ben Bassat, 43, who was working on an agricultural contract in the western city of Guadalajara, was set free last Saturday after his abductors were paid a $90,000 ransom, a spokesman for the state attorney general's office in Guadalajara told Reuters.
His kidnap -- part of a growing wave of abductions in Mexico -- was kept completely out of the media, and Mexican police were ordered by Bassat's employers in Mexico to stay out of the negotiations.
"They said they did not want the police involved," the spokesman, Sergio Villa Perez, said late on Wednesday.
The man who said he carried out the rescue was Tzachi Weintraub, an Israeli living in New York who describes his business as "troubleshooting in very unusual situations."
He said he kept trigger-happy Mexican police out of the operation "because we didn't want to risk Uri's life."

The way that he carried out negotiations is murky, however. He told Reuters in a telephone interview from New York that at one stage he threatened the kidnappers with force. "They knew it was just a matter of days before we stormed the place," he said.
However, when asked if he was armed, he replied, "Remember, I was just a tourist there." But he added: "I was prepared to use any way that I could find to release Uri."
Bassat, who was seized on Feb. 26, was held in a run-down house in a Guadalajara suburb, was not mistreated and was resting in New York, Weintraub said.

He said he persuaded the abductors by telephone to drop their ransom demand from $2 million to $90,000, and once Bassat was freed, he gave statements to Mexican police then was quickly whisked out of the country.

Mexican officials, evidently annoyed at being excluded from the negotiations, said they were carrying out their own investigation. Villa Perez expressed concern that Bassat had left Mexico so abruptly.
He said there had been six kidnappings of Mexicans in Guadalajara this year, and in all cases police had managed to obtain the release of the victims without a ransom payment.
Police in Guadalajara have a tainted track record, however. Last year, state police shot and killed a teenage girl in a disastrous attempt to free her from her kidnappers.
Kidnappings have been on the rise in Mexico since the economy nearly collapsed after a devaluation in 1994.
Last August, the Japanese head of a U.S. subsidiary of Japan's Sanyo Electric Co. was kidnapped for nine days in the northern border city of Tijuana.
